extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the MPEP two-step analysis, including how to evaluate product and process claims for judicial exceptions (laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas) and practical application/preemption issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step subject matter eligibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two criteria for determining subject matter eligibility and both must be satisfied: (1) the claimed invention must be directed to one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter), and (2) the claimed invention must not be wholly directed to subject matter encompassing a judicially recognized exception (laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two-step analysis to evaluate claims. Both steps must be considered; if Step 1 is not met the claim is ineligible, but Step 2 should still be conducted if an amendment might cure the defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category — Process
rubrics_metrics.description: A process is an act, or a series of acts or steps (a mode of treatment of certain materials to produce a given result).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: Gottschalk v. Benson; Minton; 35 U.S.C. 100(b); Bilski v. Kappos. Not every method is statutory; process claims must often be limited to a particular practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category — Machine
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine is a concrete thing, consisting of parts, or of certain devices and combination of devices — includes mechanical devices or combinations of devices to perform a function and produce a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes electrical, electronic, optical, acoustic devices; apparatus is not significantly different from machine. See Burr v. Duryee; Corning v. Burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category — Manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacture is an article produced from raw or prepared materials by giving new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations (whether by handlabor or machinery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited Diamond v. Chakrabarty and Am. Fruit Growers examples; tangible articles produced by human intervention qualify as manufactures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category — Composition of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Compositions of matter include all compositions of two or more substances and composite articles (chemical unions, mechanical mixtures; gases, fluids, powders, solids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited Chakrabarty; tangible chemical/compound compositions fall in this category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-statutory examples (what is not a statutory category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting examples of claims that are not directed to one of the statutory categories include: transitory signal transmissions (propagating electrical/electromagnetic signal per se), naturally occurring organisms, a human per se, legal contractual agreements, games defined as rules, a computer program per se, a company, and a mere arrangement of printed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is directed to these non-statutory items it should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Examples and case citations provided (In re Nuijten; Chakrabarty; AIA; In re Ferguson; Gottschalk v. Benson; In re Miller).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that cover both statutory and non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (under the broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification and a person of ordinary skill) embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: machine readable media that could encompass a compact disc (statutory) or a carrier wave (transitory signal, non-statutory) should be rejected under §101. If claim could be amended to remove the non-statutory embodiment, still perform Step 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions and preemption concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicially recognized exceptions — laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas — are not patentable; claims wholly directed to these exceptions are ineligible. The basic tools of scientific and technological work are free to all and not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claimed subject matter 'wholly embraces' an exception. Examples: natural laws, mathematical formulas, E=mc^2, Newton's law of gravity. Preemption (covering substantially all uses) is a central concern: claims that would preempt an approach across fields are likely abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is limited to a particular practical application of a judicial exception (i.e., how the exception is applied in a real world product or process) may be patent-eligible; a practical application is not merely the result achieved but concrete application showing integration into real-world use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the claim as a whole. Evidence of practical application (tangible structure, integration of law-of-nature into steps) indicates the subject matter is not abstract. See Ultramercial v. Hulu example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product claims — tangible embodiment requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed product (machine, manufacture, composition) does not recite tangible limitations under the broadest reasonable interpretation, it may wholly embrace a judicial exception; tangible structural limitations are evidence of a particular practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A machine 'comprising a plurality of structural elements' that work together shows tangible embodiment and likely eligibility; a machine claiming only the operating principle (e.g., 'operates in accordance with F=ma') without structural elements would be ineligible. Non-transitory tangible computer-readable media with structural limitations can be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption evaluation for product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying a practical application, evaluate whether the claim impermissibly covers substantially all practical applications of the judicial exception; if so, it is not patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim covers only one limited application, it is more likely eligible. Consider scope and whether others could make use of the underlying concept in other practical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process (method) claims must be limited to a particular practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim to be statutory must be limited to a particular practical application so that it does not simply claim an abstract idea or preempt all uses of a law of nature or physical phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The machine-or-transformation test remains a useful investigative tool but is not the sole test (Bilski). Recitation of structure or transformative steps often supports eligibility; however, mere field-of-use or token post-solution components do not save a claim (Flook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation and related factors for method claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider when evaluating whether a method claim is directed to an abstract idea include inquiries from the machine-or-transformation test and other inquiries gleaned from precedent (these are illustrative, not exclusive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of such factors are listed and should be weighed together rather than relying on a single factor. New factors may develop for emerging technologies; examiners should adapt as law evolves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor: involvement of a particular machine or apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the method involves or is executed by a particular machine or apparatus is a key factor: claims tied to a particular machine are less likely to be abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess particularity (specific identifiable machine vs 'any machine'), whether the machine is programmed to perform the claimed steps (programming can create a special purpose machine), and whether the machine's role imposes meaningful limits. Citations: Bilski, In re Alappat, Ultramercial, DealerTrack v. Huber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subfactors for machine involvement (particularity, implementation, extrasolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a machine or apparatus is recited, consider (a) particularity or generality of elements, (b) whether the machine implements the steps (integral use) versus being merely an object on which the method operates, and (c) whether the machine's involvement is extrasolution activity or merely a field-of-use limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular machines or machines programmed to perform steps weigh toward eligibility. Mere use of the Internet as a data source or data-gathering steps that are conventional weigh against eligibility (see Cybersource v. Retail Decisions). Field-of-use and insignificant extra-solution activities do not impose meaningful limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor: transformation of an article
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed process transforms a particular article into a different state or thing (transformation prong of the machine-or-transformation test) is relevant evidence in favor of eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claimed process that effects a physical transformation of an article is likely statutory; the MOT test is an important investigative tool but not exclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing factors and case-by-case balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant factors (both favoring and opposing eligibility) should be weighed together; each case will present different factors and it is improper to conclude based on one factor while ignoring others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that only some factors may be present in any application; examiners should consider the totality of evidence and adapt to new precedents and technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a §101 rejection (how to articulate)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim fails the inquiry that tests whether additional features provide a practical application (Inquiry 3), the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as directed to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection should: identify the natural principle or judicial exception; explain that the claim is effectively directed to that principle; and explain why additional claim features or combinations fail to integrate the principle into a practical application or fail to be 'significantly more' than the principle itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating applicant's response to a §101 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper response may amend or add claim limitations that integrate the natural principle into the process/product (practical application) and limit the claim beyond the principle plus routine steps; persuasive arguments may show the additional steps add 'significantly more' or are not routine/conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: constructing a sanitizing device using UV light with integrated steps (not simply 'expose to sunlight'); adding novel testing or treatment steps beyond routine blood testing. Demonstrating steps are not conventional can be persuasive. Refer to 2012 Interim Procedure for further examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented claims — significance of programming and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely adding a 'computer-aided' limitation or reciting a general purpose computer is insufficient to render an abstract idea patent-eligible unless the claim clearly conveys that the computer is programmed to perform the claimed steps (creating a special purpose computer) or otherwise shows meaningful technical implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must indicate how a computer aids the method, the extent of the computer's role, or the significance of the computer to performance; silent or generic recitation of a computer will weigh against eligibility (DealerTrack v. Huber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-use and 'insignificant extra-solution activity' guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Field-of-use limitations (e.g., 'for use with a machine' or 'for transforming an article') and insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., generic data-gathering) do not impose meaningful limits on the claim and do not make an abstract idea patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish meaningful structural/operational limitations from mere environment or conventional pre/post-solution activity. Such insignificant elements should not be treated as conferring patent eligibility (citing Bilski, Parker v. Flook, Cybersource).
